I get the law. I'm sure Ford, GM, Honda, Toyota, etc would love to sell direct and cut out the middle man. Considering dealerships don't have a corporation larger than a hand full of states I think you can legitimately call these organizations "medium sized businesses". Especially in areas around Detroit it's easy to see that they'd want their investments of million dollar facilities protected against being strong armed out by the people making their products.

At the same time I think it's very curious that, as a new car company, Tesla seems unwilling to partner with existing dealerships with infrastructure already in place. I'd be surprised the majority of dealerships weren't chomping at the bit to buy some Tesla cars. It is a bold strategy to want to invest in factories as well as point of sale facilities when there are so many places to sell your product already.

I'm not a libertarian, but I think this is one of the most clear-cut cases against government interference. Suppose car companies are allowed to sell direct to the consumer and all dealerships disappear. What part of buying a car gets worse for the consumer? Why should the law make a transaction worse for both of the parties involved in it by mandating the inclusion and payment of a third party who adds no value?

If you believe in capitalism then the price of the car will not change regardless if the car is sold through a dealership or direct to the consumer. In capitalism: the consumer, i.e. the market sets the price. How much or how little overhead really only dictates whether or not a product is available (producers need to make a profit). How much profit is really up to how much the market is willing to spend on the product.

Anybody who says adding overhead price to a product increases the price in a capitalist economy doesn't really believe in capitalism. They're really just laying down a marketing excuse to raise the price and see if the market is willing to accept that price. If they do accept the price, then the increase remains. If they don't accept the price then the price will fall back to what the market is willing to pay.
If it really doesn't make a difference, then why not allow both sales mechanisms?

Protect investments, protect jobs, and regulate a diverse market. While were 20 steps away from an auto cartel, if car companies would be able to control manufacturing to point of sale, and gain considerable market control and inflate the price. The market is willing to spend a lot more for a product when the market is controlled by a limited number of entities. Overall it's worse for the consumer.

Isn't the point of capitalism that the consumer gets to decide what's worse for the consumer?

How is Telsa less able to mark up their prices to sell to a bunch of dealerships than to a bunch of consumers?

Also, if inserting this extra layer of people who can't make a car between the manufacturers and the consumer is so beneficial, why not insert a second? Only tier 1 resellers can buy from the manufacturer and sell to tier 2 resellers, and only tier 2 resellers can sell to consumers. Shouldn't this also create jobs and keep prices down?
